first_impression.reaction: My assistant flagged this because my fiance's family is Cantonese, from Sydney. The headline is a bit 'listicle' for my taste, but the opening sentence redeems it: "In a family, they are a sequence: gifts carried to the bride's home weeks ahead, a comb drawn through the hair by candlelight, a door that only opens once the groom has earned it, and cups of tea offered on bended knee." That's composed and respectful. I'd let her summarise it, then read the tea ceremony part myself.

journey.section: Chinese wedding customs differ by family and region
journey.quote: There is no single traditional Chinese wedding.
journey.reaction: Correct, and important. His mother would close the page if it told her what 'Chinese' families do as if we were all one.

journey.section: Chinese wedding customs differ by family and region
journey.quote: Where a custom is passed on by word of mouth rather than documented, we say it is "often told", and we leave its meaning to your family.
journey.reaction: Cultural awareness without stereotyping. That's what I look for in anyone who will be in the room with our elders.

journey.quote: Take them lightly, but take them early: Singapore's National Library Board notes that hotel function rooms tend to be fully booked on dates seen as auspicious.
journey.reaction: Useful. For us that means the family's chosen date drives everything, including whether we can get the whole property. It stops short of saying they can secure exclusive use on a date like that.

journey.section: 5. Door games at the bride's home
journey.quote: If either family is Teochew, ask early, because it moves hair and make-up into the small hours.
journey.reaction: This sounds like someone who has actually built a run sheet. Understated, practical.

journey.section: 6. Who serves whom, and in what order
journey.quote: Agree the list of elders in advance, and set out a cushion for kneeling.
journey.reaction: Fine for a family of twenty. With 300 guests, two tea sittings and travel between two homes, the real question is cars, timing and who keeps photographers out. A cushion is not my concern; the convoy is.

journey.quote: We leave the sums to them.
journey.reaction: Good. No money talk, no 'value'. That restraint reads as premium.

journey.quote: China does not recognise dual nationality, and dual nationals who don't enter on their Australian passport may be unable to get Australian consular help.
journey.reaction: Frank, and relevant to families like ours with several passports. But safety for us also means our own security working with the venue's, and that isn't mentioned.

journey.quote: If China is one option among several, see [destination weddings in Asia](/destinations/asia), [the do's and don'ts of Asian destination weddings](/the-dos-and-donts-of-asian-destination-weddings) and our [destination wedding packages](/destination-wedding-packages).
journey.reaction: 'Packages' again. It tells me I'd be put in a tier. My assistant wouldn't click it.

journey.section: Bringing Chinese customs to a wedding at home
journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Grown-up and unhurried. One contact suits how we work. Still nothing on discretion or scale.

unanswered_questions: Has Wedded Wonderland delivered a Chinese or Chinese-Australian wedding of 200 to 400 guests, with two tea sittings and a full banquet?
Can they secure exclusive use of a hotel or estate on an auspicious date, when function rooms are already in demand?
How do they handle privacy: NDAs, guest phone policies, keeping vendors off social media?
Can they coordinate private transfers between two family homes on the morning, and work alongside our own security team?
Do they work with banquet chefs who can build a Cantonese menu with the elders, at this scale?
Is there a private or referral channel to someone senior, rather than a general advisor link?

turn_offs_found.quote: If China is one option among several, see [destination weddings in Asia](/destinations/asia), [the do's and don'ts of Asian destination weddings](/the-dos-and-donts-of-asian-destination-weddings) and our [destination wedding packages](/destination-wedding-packages).
turn_offs_found.why: Package language makes it sound like a standard tier, which is exactly what we don't want.

would_share_with: My fiance's mother, for the tea ceremony order and the hair-combing section
My assistant, to file with the planner shortlist notes

cta_reaction.quote: If you are planning a wedding in China, or a Chinese-Australian celebration at home, you can [speak with a Wedded Advisor](/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=chinese-wedding-traditions&utm_content=bridge).
cta_reaction.why: Calm, no hard sell, and the closing 'a calm place to start' suits me. But I don't fill in web forms. If my assistant could arrange a private introduction, I'd take a call. On this page alone there's no evidence of scale or discretion.

top_3_changes: Swap the 'destination wedding packages' link for a page that doesn't say 'packages', such as a bespoke or concierge planning page.
Add one understated line near the tea ceremony or bridge saying the team handles exclusive use, transfers between family homes and security liaison for larger family weddings, if that's true.
Mention discretion or privacy in the CTA, and offer a private conversation rather than only a general advisor link.
